```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE,
                     fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = 110)
options(width = 85)
# Helpers for numbers quoted in the text (nothing below is typed in by hand).
quoted <- function(x) {
  x <- paste0("\u201c", x, "\u201d")
  if (length(x) < 2) x else paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
}
num <- function(x, digits = 1) ifelse(is.finite(x), formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f", big.mark = ","), "not estimated")
count <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
one_line <- function(x) gsub("\\s*\n\\s*", " ", as.character(x))
```

This tutorial shows how to explore whether the effect of one variable on another is larger for some people than for others. You need three things:

- a **dependent variable (Y)**, the outcome you want to explain: numeric, either continuous or binary (0/1);
- an **independent variable (W)**, whose effect on Y you want to study: two groups, such as treated and untreated, or a number, such as hours of use (see the [README](../README.md#a-numeric-independent-variable));
- **characteristics (X)** that might moderate the effect, that is, make it larger or smaller.

A causal forest estimates the effect of W for people with different characteristics and points to patterns worth investigating.

The example uses the 2024 General Social Survey (GSS). Y is a 0–100 rating of Donald Trump. W compares respondents who identify as conservative with those who identify as liberal or moderate. Political identification was not randomly assigned, so we read the results as **adjusted associations**, not causal effects.

There are four steps: choose variables, run the forest, compare groups and export results. The [app](../README.md#the-app) follows the same steps without code.

## 1. Choose variables

Install the package and `gssr` as described in the [README](../README.md#installation). Then load the package and download the example:

```{r load}
library(heterogeneity)
gss <- load_gss2024()
```

`load_gss2024()` downloads the current GSS 2024 release and prepares it, checking every recode against the GSS category labels; nothing is stored in the package. `gss$data` has one row for each of the `r count(nrow(gss$data))` respondents with a value for both Y and W. `gss$covariates` names `r length(gss$covariates)` demographic, socioeconomic, religious, attitudinal and wellbeing characteristics, and `gss$codebook` describes every column:

```{r codebook}
gss$codebook[gss$codebook$variable %in% c("rating_trump", "conservative", "age", "lkelyvot"), ]
```

```{r missing-numbers, include=FALSE}
share_missing <- colMeans(is.na(gss$data[gss$covariates]))
most_missing <- names(which.max(share_missing))
```

Choose characteristics that make sense for your question. Numbers are treated as ordered values, so turn unordered codes (such as region codes) into text or factors first; text columns are turned into 0/1 indicators automatically. If you want to read the results causally, use only characteristics that W could not have changed.

**Keep missing characteristics.** The forest handles missing values directly, so nothing needs to be filled in. Here the characteristic missing most often is `r quoted(gss$labels[[most_missing]])`, for `r num(100 * share_missing[[most_missing]])`% of respondents. This avoids inventing values, but it does not remove bias when values are missing for systematic reasons. Rows missing Y or W (or a supplied weight or cluster) are left out, and the report lists every such change.

## 2. Run the forest

One call fits the forest, and printing the report shows a summary and draws three plots. The labels are optional; here they come from the example.

```{r report, fig.keep="none"}
report <- explore_heterogeneity(
  data = gss$data, y = "rating_trump", w = "conservative",
  x = gss$covariates, ids = "id",
  labels = gss$labels, value_labels = gss$value_labels,
  effect_label = gss$effect_label
)
report
```

```{r report-numbers, include=FALSE}
groups <- report$settings$w_labels
direction <- if (report$ate$estimate >= 0) "higher" else "lower"
profiles <- plot(report, "profiles")$data
ends <- range(profiles$quintile)
low <- profiles[profiles$quintile == ends[1], ]
high <- profiles[profiles$quintile == ends[2], ]
high <- high[match(low$feature, high$feature), ]
widest <- which.max(abs(high$z - low$z))
below <- mean(report$cates$cate_estimate < 0)
below_text <- if (below == 0) "every prediction is above 0" else if (below == 1) "every prediction is below 0" else
  sprintf("%s%% of the predictions are below 0", num(100 * below, 0))
rows <- c(importance = nrow(report$moderators), profiles = nrow(report$feature_map))
```

**The summary.** The average adjusted difference is **`r num(abs(report$ate$estimate))` rating points**: on average, `r tolower(groups[2])` respondents rate Trump `r num(abs(report$ate$estimate))` points `r direction` than `r tolower(groups[1])` respondents with similar characteristics. The report calls this the average treatment effect, the standard name for the quantity; because W was not randomly assigned here, it is an adjusted association rather than a causal effect. It also differs from simply subtracting the two group means, because it compares people with similar characteristics.

In standard deviations the average is **`r num(report$ate$standardized, 2)`**: the difference divided by how much ratings vary within the two groups, before adjustment (one standard deviation is `r num(report$ate$sd_y)` points). This standardized effect size can be compared across outcomes measured in different units. Everything else stays in rating points; dividing by `report$ate$sd_y` converts any of it.

The forest's predictions range from `r num(report$prediction_range[1])` to `r num(report$prediction_range[2])` points. They come from `r count(report$settings$num_trees)` honest trees: each tree uses one part of the data to choose its splits and another part to estimate the differences, and each respondent's prediction comes only from trees grown without them ("out-of-bag"). The overall and group averages use doubly robust scores, which combine the predictions with the observed ratings. The candidate moderators are the characteristics the forest used most in its splits, and the data notes list everything that was changed or left out.

Below, the three plots are shown one at a time, each with its explanation. `plot(report)`, `plot(report, "importance")` and `plot(report, "profiles")` draw them on their own, for example to save one.

```{r plot-1}
plot(report)
```

**Plot 1: how much do predicted differences vary?** The histogram shows each respondent's predicted difference, with the number of bins chosen from the data (the Freedman–Diaconis rule). As in the heatmaps, the colours deepen with distance from 0. Teal bars, above 0, are predictions in which `r tolower(groups[2])` respondents rate Trump higher than `r tolower(groups[1])` respondents with similar characteristics, and the further above 0, the deeper the teal; red bars, below 0, would show the reverse. Here `r below_text`. These are model predictions: part of their spread is estimation noise, so the plot is not the true distribution of effects, and the smallest and largest predictions are the least reliable.

```{r plot-2, fig.height = 1.2 + 0.2 * rows[["importance"]]}
plot(report, "importance")
```

**Plot 2: which candidate moderators did the forest use most?** The chart ranks all `r rows[["importance"]]` characteristics. The top-ranked one is **`r report$moderators$label[1]`**. Importance measures how often, and how early, the forest split on a characteristic. That makes it a candidate moderator, not a proven one: importance does not say whether the difference rises or falls with the characteristic, and related characteristics share importance. For a text characteristic, the importance of its indicators is added together.

```{r plot-3, fig.height = 1.4 + 0.24 * rows[["profiles"]]}
plot(report, "profiles")
```

**Plot 3: who has smaller and larger predictions?** Each row is a characteristic, in order of importance (a text characteristic gets one row per category). Each column is a prediction group: the respondents are sorted by their predictions and split into up to five groups of about equal size. A cell shows the group's average z-score: the value minus the sample mean, divided by the standard deviation. So 0 is the sample average, and negative cells are below it and positive cells above it, on the same scale for every characteristic. For example, `r quoted(one_line(low$label[widest]))` averages `r sprintf("%+.2f", low$z[widest])` in the group with the smallest predictions and `r sprintf("%+.2f", high$z[widest])` in the group with the largest. Missing values are ignored. Because the groups are formed by sorting the predictions, some separation comes from the sorting itself: use this plot to describe the forest's pattern, and check meaningful groups in step 3.

A few options are worth knowing. In a randomized experiment, supply the known probability of being in the group coded 1, such as `W_hat = 0.5`; otherwise, as here, the forest estimates it. Survey weights and clusters can be supplied as `weights = "svy_weight"` and `clusters = "psu_cluster"`; this illustration is unweighted, so it describes these respondents. The default seed (`r format(report$settings$seed, scientific = FALSE)`) makes the results reproducible. With many characteristics, `top_n` limits the importance and profile plots, for example `plot(report, "importance", top_n = 10)`.

## 3. Compare groups

`effect_by()` is the focused check: it estimates the adjusted difference within the groups of one characteristic. Likelihood of voting is a natural first choice here, because it ranks `r which(report$moderators$variable == "lkelyvot")` of `r nrow(report$moderators)` in importance.

```{r voting-table}
voting <- effect_by(report, "lkelyvot")
voting
```

```{r voting-numbers, include=FALSE}
observed <- voting[voting$lkelyvot != "(Missing)", ]
lowest <- observed[1, ]
highest <- observed[nrow(observed), ]
category <- function(code) tolower(gss$value_labels$lkelyvot[[as.character(code)]])
```

Each row is a group of respondents, labelled by its code (the codebook above gives the meaning). `n_control` counts the `r tolower(groups[1])` respondents in the group and `n_treated` the `r tolower(groups[2])` ones. A group with fewer than 30 respondents, or with only one group of W, gets no estimate, and its `status` says why. The difference is `r num(lowest$estimate)` points among respondents who are `r category(lowest$lkelyvot)` to vote and `r num(highest$estimate)` among those who are `r category(highest$lkelyvot)`. The table includes respondents with a missing answer as a group of their own; the plot leaves them out:

```{r voting-plot}
plot(voting)
```

These groups also differ in other ways, so the plot does not show what would happen if someone's likelihood of voting changed. Check characteristics your theory names as well as the top-ranked ones:

```{r age-plot}
age <- effect_by(report, "age")
plot(age)
```

```{r age-numbers, include=FALSE}
age_observed <- age[age$age != "(Missing)", ]
first_age <- age_observed[1, ]
last_age <- age_observed[nrow(age_observed), ]
```

Age is cut into up to five groups of about equal size, labelled by the ages they contain. The difference is `r num(first_age$estimate)` points for ages `r as.character(first_age$age)` and `r num(last_age$estimate)` for ages `r as.character(last_age$age)`. These describe age groups, not the effect of growing older, and the group boundaries are not thresholds.

Two characteristics give a heatmap:

```{r two-way, fig.height=6}
plot(effect_by(report, "lkelyvot", "income16"))
```

With two characteristics, numeric ones are cut into three groups each. Income is recorded in ordered categories, not dollar amounts; `gss$codebook` gives their meaning. Each cell shows an adjusted difference and its number of respondents, coloured around the overall average. Grey cells have too few respondents, or only one group of W, to be estimated. The heatmap leaves out respondents missing either characteristic; the table from `effect_by(report, "lkelyvot", "income16")` includes them.

## 4. Export results

Save the estimates and predictions as ordinary CSV files:

```{r export, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(effect_by(report, "age"), "age_groups.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(report$moderators, "importance.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(report$cates, "predictions.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

A short report can say:

> Among `r count(report$settings$n)` GSS respondents, those identifying as conservative rated Trump `r num(abs(report$ate$estimate))` points (`r num(abs(report$ate$standardized), 2)` standard deviations) `r direction`, on average, than liberal or moderate respondents with similar characteristics. The characteristics the forest used most were `r quoted(report$moderators$label[1:3])`. Across voting-likelihood groups, the adjusted difference ranged from `r num(min(observed$estimate, na.rm = TRUE))` to `r num(max(observed$estimate, na.rm = TRUE))` points. The analysis was unweighted, and missing characteristics were kept for the forest rather than filled in. These patterns are exploratory: predictions describe profiles and include noise.

Add the group estimates and counts relevant to your question. A causal reading needs a defensible research design, comparable groups and suitable characteristics; the GSS example makes no causal claim.

The [grf guide](https://grf-labs.github.io/grf/articles/grf_guide.html) explains the underlying method and its handling of missing values. The [Stanford tutorial](https://bookdown.org/stanfordgsbsilab/ml-ci-tutorial/hte-i-binary-treatment.html) gives more background.

```{r versions, echo=FALSE}
data.frame(Component = c("R", "heterogeneity", "grf", "gssr"),
           Version = c(as.character(getRversion()), vapply(c("heterogeneity", "grf", "gssr"),
                                                           function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)), "", USE.NAMES = FALSE)))
```
